statement: git checkout -B lane/arc-20 origin/rust-build failed with 'already used by worktree' because a predecessor session's worktree (agent-a4b04bbfdebf621b5) had checked out the branch and then died at startup before doing any work (still at the pre-build base commit a6a1514, not the required 4bb883d). This was a dead orphaned worktree registration, not a live coordination-ledger lock conflict.
why: git worktree add/checkout -B ties a branch to exactly one worktree directory at a time; a killed session leaves that tie dangling even though nothing was committed. The coordination ledger (claim/release) is a separate mechanism from git's own worktree-branch binding and does not clean up the latter.
howToApply: Before assuming a branch conflict is a live-lane fight, run `git worktree list` and inspect the commit the conflicting worktree is pinned at. If it matches the pre-work base SHA (no commits beyond the checkout point) and the task says the predecessor was killed with nothing to salvage, it is safe to `git worktree remove --force <path>` + `git worktree prune` and retake the branch — this is a git-level cleanup, not a coordination-ledger override, so it does not need an editIntent or hub notification beyond mentioning it in started-mail for visibility.

evidence.ref: git worktree list output at session start

statement: A crate meant to host several sequentially-landing feature packs (enforcer-plan: b01..b06 + x05) cannot pre-declare `pub mod scaffolder;` etc. for modules that don't exist yet -- `mod` statements require the file to exist or the crate fails to compile. The correct skeleton pattern is: ship only the modules the skeleton lane itself owns (here, `error.rs`), and put the full mount map (which future module owns which file, in what order) into the crate's top-level `//!` doc comment as prose, not as commented-out `mod` lines.
why: The workpack's stop-rule forbids arc-20 from creating b01-b06's files, but Rust's module system has no way to declare a module without its backing file existing. Commented-out `pub mod` lines would bit-rot (nothing forces a feature pack to notice/uncomment the right one, and clippy/fmt don't check comments), whereas a doc-comment mount map is read by the human/agent landing each feature pack as the actual instruction for what one-line addition to make to lib.rs.
howToApply: When laying a skeleton crate for future disjoint feature packs, keep lib.rs compiling with only your own modules active, and write the full future-module list (name, owning workpack id, one-line responsibility, non-goals) into the crate doc comment. Each feature pack's own job then includes adding exactly one `pub mod <name>;` line to lib.rs when it lands -- expect that file to be touched by multiple lanes sequentially, which is fine since each touch is a single appended line, not a structural rewrite.
